title: Error, Waste, Abuse, and Fraud Distinctions

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish among error, waste, abuse, and fraud in medical billing and documentation.
- Explain the central role of intent, including knowing, willful, reckless, and deliberate-ignorance standards, in separating fraud from error, waste, and abuse.
- Recognize how accurate documentation supports correct billing and reveals when claims are unsupported or misrepresented.
- Apply correct escalation responsibilities when an error, overpayment, or suspected fraud or abuse is identified.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

An error is like dialing the wrong phone number by accident. Nobody meant to do it, and it can be fixed once it is noticed.

### Question 2

Waste is like leaving all the lights on in an empty house. It wastes resources, but it is not a crime; it is just inefficient.

### Question 3

Abuse is like bending the rules in a board game a little too far without being caught lying. It is questionable, but no one has proven you meant to cheat.

### Question 4

Fraud is like handing in a receipt for something you never bought just to get money back. You know it is false, and you do it on purpose.

### Question 5

Fraud is like a lie you tell on purpose, while an error is an accident. What matters is whether the person meant to do it, not how big it was.

### Question 6

Errors and waste are like spilling a drink and leaving the water running; both are accidental or careless, but neither is meant to hurt anyone.

### Question 7

Fraud is the only category that needs proof that a person meant to do something wrong on purpose.

### Question 8

Mixing up two numbers by accident is like dialing a phone number wrong; it is a simple mistake, not a scheme.

### Question 9

Reordering supplies you already have is like buying more milk when the fridge is already full. It wastes money but is not a crime.

### Question 10

Abuse is like always rounding up a bill a little and hoping no one checks. It looks questionable, but no one has proven it was done on purpose.

### Question 11

Billing for a service that never happened is like charging someone for a meal you never served. It is a lie told on purpose.

### Question 12

Fraud is like charging a customer for a repair you never made. You are getting paid for something that did not happen.

### Question 13

Forgetting the modifier is like forgetting to add a stamp to a letter; it simply does not go through until you fix it.

### Question 14

Getting the same test twice with no reason is like printing two copies of a page you only need once; it wastes resources.

### Question 15

Fraud, waste, and abuse are all ways money gets paid when it should not have been, so they are grouped as improper payments.

### Question 16

You cannot read someone's mind, so instead people look at clues like repeated patterns and records to figure out what they meant to do.

### Question 17

A typo you fix right away is an accident; doing something on purpose to get extra money is a different story.

### Question 18

Waste is a leaky pipe, not a theft, so you fix the pipe instead of calling the police.

### Question 19

Abuse and fraud look similar, but fraud is when you can prove the person meant to cheat; abuse is when it looks wrong but you cannot prove intent.

### Question 20

If you catch a mistake, you tell the person in charge so it gets fixed the right way instead of hiding it or fixing it secretly.

### Question 21

If you find out you got paid too much and keep doing it on purpose, you are now cheating instead of making a mistake.

### Question 22

Deliberate ignorance is like covering your eyes so you can say you did not see. That does not excuse you.

### Question 23

This is like handing in homework answers you know are copied, hoping the teacher will not check. You know it is wrong.

### Question 24

The chart is like the receipt that proves what really happened; without it, no one can tell if a bill is honest.

### Question 25

Bill only what is written down as really happening, like only charging for the toppings actually on the pizza.

### Question 26

When you are not sure, tell the grown-up in charge instead of guessing, hiding it, or blaming someone loudly.

### Question 27

If someone asks you to do something dishonest, the right move is to say no and tell a trusted supervisor.

### Question 28

If the same mistake keeps happening and it always helps the practice, it is probably not a mistake at all.

### Question 29

Changing the record to make a bill look right is like changing your test answers after grading to get a better score.

### Question 30

A proper correction is like crossing out a word with a single line and writing the fix next to it, so everyone can still see what changed.

### Question 31

Backdating is like writing yesterday's date on today's homework; it makes it look like you did it earlier than you really did.

### Question 32

Copying the same note every time is like turning in the same essay for every assignment; it does not show what really happened each time.

### Question 33

If the store gives you too much change, the right thing is to give it back, not to keep it or spend it.

### Question 34

What matters is whether someone meant to do it wrong, not any of the details around the claim.

### Question 35

Using the expensive tape when cheap tape works is wasteful, but it is not a lie meant to steal money.

### Question 36

If there is no receipt for a charge, you do not charge it; you find out what really happened first.

### Question 37

If the same rule keeps getting bent in a way that always helps one side, it is worth checking whether it is really an accident.

### Question 38

You treat a spilt drink, a leaky faucet, and a broken window differently, so you sort out what kind of problem it is first.

### Question 39

One little typo fixed right away is just an accident, nothing more.

### Question 40

Erasing your answer to hide a mistake makes things worse, because now it looks like you are hiding something.

### Question 41

If you think something might be wrong, check it instead of shrugging and sending it anyway.

### Question 42

Abuse is like always using the express lane when your cart is full; it looks wrong but no one has proven you meant to cheat.

### Question 43

Making up a pretend customer to collect money is clearly a lie, and that is fraud.

### Question 44

Splitting a bill into extra charges could be a mistake, a bad habit, or a scheme; what matters is whether it was done on purpose.

### Question 45

If you see charges on days the shop was closed, you tell a manager, because something is not right.

### Question 46

If you honestly tell about a problem, you should be safe from being punished for speaking up.

### Question 47

The compliance program is like the office that listens when something important might be wrong and figures out what to do.

### Question 48

If you know it is a lie, saying no and telling the right person is the only safe choice, no matter who asked.

### Question 49

A kickback is like a secret payment to steer customers; it is not a fair way to do business.

### Question 50

If the person sending you to a store also owns that store, it can be a problem worth flagging.

### Question 51

An honest mistake gets fixed and learned from, while a deliberate lie gets punished.

### Question 52

Cheating a government program can mean big fines and being kicked out of the program entirely.

### Question 53

A few typos are accidents, but the same error in almost half of all claims, always helping the same side, looks planned.

### Question 54

Writing things down correctly is how you prove you did your job honestly, like keeping a clear receipt.

### Question 55

Changing the label to get a higher price when the facts did not change is like repricing an item to charge more.

### Question 56

You reduce waste by turning off lights and fixing leaks, not by punishing people.

### Question 57

Not every accident is a crime, and calling it one is unfair and unhelpful.

### Question 58

Running extra tests just to make money is wasteful and unfair, like charging for work that was not needed.

### Question 59

If everyone is doing something that looks wrong, the safe move is to tell the right person, not to join in.

### Question 60

If you get paid twice for one job, you give the extra back, even if it was a mistake.

### Question 61

It is like the difference between an accident, a mess, bending the rules, and a deliberate lie, in that order.

### Question 62

Since you cannot see inside someone's head, you figure out what they meant by watching what they did over and over.

### Question 63

Fixing your mistake and telling someone right away proves it was an accident, not a scheme.

### Question 64

The chart is like a diary of what really happened, and the bill has to match it.

### Question 65

If someone asks you to hide money that does not belong to you, the safe choice is to say no and tell the right person.

### Question 66

Waste is like running the air conditioner with the windows open; it wastes money but no one is trying to steal.

### Question 67

If the price list is old, everyone uses the wrong price by accident; you fix the list and teach everyone the new one.

### Question 68

Abuse gets a warning and a fix; fraud gets serious consequences, because one is questionable and the other is a knowing lie.

### Question 69

If you see something that looks wrong, tell the right person quietly and properly instead of making a scene or looking away.

### Question 70

Knowing the rules helps everyone spot problems early, like learning the rules of a game before playing.

### Question 71

A charge on a day the shop was closed is a big warning sign that something is not right.

### Question 72

One little typo fixed right away is an accident, while the others are things people did on purpose.

### Question 73

Own the mistake and fix it right away; hiding it is what turns an accident into a problem.

### Question 74

A scheme is a plan to cheat over time, not a one-time accident.

### Question 75

Audits are like regular checkups for the billing process, catching small problems before they get big.

### Question 76

The assistant helps by being careful and efficient and telling the boss when something is being wasted.

### Question 77

You cannot get out of trouble by covering your eyes and saying you did not see anything.

### Question 78

Writing down a sickness the patient does not have to get paid is a lie, and the right answer is to refuse and tell someone.

### Question 79

Fraud is a lie on purpose; an error is an accident. That is the whole difference.

### Question 80

If an order seems off, ask about it and follow the rules, instead of changing things or pretending not to see it.

### Question 81

Even the person who types the numbers is part of making sure the bill is honest, so the rules matter to everyone.

### Question 82

When you are not sure what something is, ask someone who knows instead of guessing or staying silent.

### Question 83

Charging the biggest price for every single customer no matter what they got is a sign something is wrong.

### Question 84

If you send the wrong bill, you send a corrected one; you do not pretend it never happened.

### Question 85

Fixing someone else's suspicious work in secret is like erasing a clue at a crime scene; it makes you part of the problem.
